extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), applicants, and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for filing and evaluating petitions under 37 CFR 1.137 to revive unintentionally or unavoidably abandoned patent applications (including requirements for replies, fees, evidence, terminal disclaimers, and timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue fee payment requirement to avoid abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Notice of Allowance requires the timely payment of the issue fee in effect on the date of its mailing to avoid abandonment of the application; if the issue fee increases before payment the Office will mail a notice requiring payment of the balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reply consisting only of payment of the issue fee or any outstanding balance thereof is not an acceptable reply in an application abandoned or patent lapsed for failure to pay the issue fee or any portion thereof. If no portion was previously submitted, the reply must be the issue fee then in effect; if a portion was previously submitted, the reply must be any outstanding balance then in effect. See In re Mills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible replies for nonprovisional application abandoned for failure to reply
rubrics_metrics.description: For a nonprovisional application abandoned for failure to reply to a final Office action, the reply required for consideration of a petition to revive must be: (A) a Notice of Appeal (and appeal fee); (B) an amendment that cancels all the rejected claims or otherwise prima facie places the application in condition for allowance; or (C) the filing of a continuing application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reply to a non-final action may be an argument or an amendment under 37 CFR 1.111; a reply under 37 CFR 1.113 to a final action must include cancellation of, or appeal from, the rejection of each claim so rejected. Filing a continuing application is a permissive reply in many cases. The Office may require filing a continuing application (or a request for further examination under 1.129(a)) where treating a reply under 1.111 or 1.113 would place an inordinate burden on the Office (e.g., long abandonment, multiple/conflicting replies, questionable compliance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office review procedure for proposed amendments filed as the reply
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proposed amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 is filed as the required reply to a final action, the Office of Petitions will normally route the amendment to the examining group to determine whether it places the application in condition for allowance prior to granting any petition to revive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner determines the reply places the application in condition for allowance, the examiner should annotate the reply 'OK to enter upon revival' and the petition will be granted if otherwise grantable. If not, the examiner completes form PTOL-303 and returns it to the Office of Petitions; the petition will not be granted if the amendment does not place the application in condition for allowance. PTOL-303 serves as advisory to the Office of Petitions and is not mailed with the petition decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of reply and post-revival review
rubrics_metrics.description: The grant of a petition under 37 CFR 1.137 is not a determination that any reply under 37 CFR 1.111 is complete; the examiner may later determine the reply is lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If, after revival, a more detailed review shows the reply lacking, the examiner should send a letter giving a 1-month shortened statutory period under 37 CFR 1.135(c) for correction; extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) are permitted. Failure to correct within the shortened period (including any extension) will result in the application being again abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition fee requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for revival of an unintentionally abandoned application or for the unintentionally delayed payment of the issue fee must be accompanied by the petition fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(m), unless the petition is filed under 35 U.S.C. 133 or 151 (on the basis of unavoidable delay), in which case the fee is set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(l).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petition fee is a statutory prerequisite to revival and is due on filing the petition; the Office will not reach the merits of any petition lacking the requisite petition fee, and the petition fee will not be refunded regardless of dismissal or denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and evidentiary differences: unintentional vs. unavoidable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions under 37 CFR 1.137(b) are evaluated under the less stringent 'unintentional delay' standard and generally require only a statement that the entire delay was unintentional; petitions under 37 CFR 1.137(a) must establish that the delay was 'unavoidable' and require documentary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 1.137(b) the Office usually accepts applicant's statement(s) describing cause of delay (and may request additional information only where questioned). For 1.137(a) a showing of unavoidable delay requires evidence concerning procedures in place to avoid the error, training and experience of responsible persons, and docketing records showing the error caused the delay. Many petitions filed under 1.137(a) are instead granted under 1.137(b) when evidence of unavoidable delay is difficult to obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of false or inappropriate statements in 1.137(b) petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office relies on the applicant's duty of candor and good faith and accepts statements that the entire delay was unintentional in the vast majority of 1.137(b) petitions without further inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing an inappropriate statement in a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b) may have adverse effects when attempting to enforce any resulting patent (e.g., inequitable conduct leading to unenforceability). The applicant (or practitioner) has obligations under 37 CFR 10.18 to inquire into the underlying facts before making such statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional delay is not 'unintentional' — examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A delay resulting from a deliberately chosen course of action on the part of the applicant is not 'unintentional' within 37 CFR 1.137(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of deliberate decisions that preclude finding unintentional delay include: (A) applicant does not consider claims patentable over outstanding references; (B) applicant does not consider allowed/patentable claims of sufficient breadth/value to justify expense; (C) applicant does not consider any patent sufficiently valuable; (D) applicant does not consider any patent to maintain an interest; (E) applicant remains interested but seeks to defer fees and prosecution expenses. A later change of mind does not convert an intentional abandonment into an unintentional delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended statement and forms for 1.137(b) petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: To expedite treatment, applicants filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b) are advised to include the statement: 'the entire delay in filing the required reply from the due date for the reply until the filing of a grantable petition pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137(b) was unintentional.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may use Office forms PTO/SB/64 or PTO/SB/64PCT for such petitions. Including the recommended statement (even when also providing a factual explanation) helps expedite processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unavoidable delay standard (reasonably prudent person) and required showing
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'unavoidable' standard is judged by a 'reasonably prudent person' test and requires demonstration that the delay was unavoidable despite ordinary care. Decisions are case-by-case, considering all facts and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An error by an employee may support unavoidable delay only if: (A) the error caused the delay; (B) a reliable business routine existed for the clerical function; and (C) the employee was sufficiently trained/experienced to make reliance reasonable (see In re Egbers). Specific examples (e.g., change of correspondence address) require evidence of due care in notifying the Office, and certain types of notification do not constitute proper notice (e.g., mere inclusion of a different address on an unrelated paper without stating a change of address).

rubrics_metrics.name: What does not constitute 'unavoidable' delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Delays resulting from lack of knowledge or improper application of the patent statute, rules of practice, or the MPEP do not constitute 'unavoidable' delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: permitting maximum extension periods to expire while awaiting a notice of allowance, failure to file papers/fees in compliance with 37 CFR 1.8 or 1.10, reliance on oral advice from PTO employees, or PTO failure to advise the applicant of a deficiency do not render a delay 'unavoidable'. Case law: Haines v. Quigg; Vincent v. Mossinghoff; Krahn; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for petitions under 1.137
rubrics_metrics.description: For a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(a) the applicant must carry the burden of proof to establish that the entire delay from the due date for the reply until the filing of a grantable petition was unavoidable. For 37 CFR 1.137(b) a statement of unintentional delay is required, but the Commissioner may require additional information and proof where there is a question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will require the showing to the satisfaction of the Commissioner for 1.137(a); for 1.137(b) the Office generally accepts the statement but may require the applicant to carry the burden of proof if doubts exist (see Application of G). Failure to carry the burden may lead to denial regardless of the original cause of abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer requirement under 37 CFR 1.137(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition under either 37 CFR 1.137(a) or 1.137(b) must be accompanied by a terminal disclaimer (and fee) in: (A) design applications; (B) nonprovisional utility applications filed before June 8, 1995; and (C) nonprovisional plant applications filed before June 8, 1995.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The terminal disclaimer must dedicate to the public a terminal part of the patent term equivalent to the period of abandonment, and must apply to any patent on continuing applications entitled to the benefit of the filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120. The terminal disclaimer requirement does not apply to lapsed patents. Filing a terminal disclaimer does not substitute for establishing unavoidable/unintentional delay. An applicant may file a petition under 37 CFR 1.183 (with fee) to request waiver of the terminal disclaimer only upon a showing of an 'extraordinary situation' in which 'justice requires' relief (e.g., no actual delay in prosecution; patent term otherwise capped). Forms PTO/SB/62 and PTO/SB/63 may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for reconsideration/review timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Any request for reconsideration or review of a decision refusing to revive an abandoned application or lapsed patent must be filed within 2 months of the decision refusing to revive or within such time set in the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless a decision indicates otherwise, the time period for requesting reconsideration or review may be extended under the provisions of 37 CFR 1.136.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness thresholds and 'delay until filing a grantable petition' considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three periods considered in evaluating a petition: (A) the delay in reply that resulted in abandonment; (B) the delay in filing an initial petition under 1.137; and (C) the delay in filing a grantable petition under 1.137. The Office generally will not question intentional delay where a petition is filed within 3 months of first notification of abandonment and within 1 year of the date of abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a petition is filed after 3 months from first notification, the Office will require a showing as to how the delay between notification and filing was 'unavoidable' (for 1.137(a)) or may require further information about how it was 'unintentional' (for 1.137(b)). If not filed within 1 year of abandonment, the Office will require information about when the applicant first became aware of abandonment and a showing how discovery of the abandoned status occurred despite due care/diligence. Applicants should include appropriate showings when filing late to avoid delays in consideration. Intentional delay in seeking revival (e.g., waiting for industry interest) precludes findings of unavoidable/unintentional delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant party whose delay is evaluated
rubrics_metrics.description: The question under 37 CFR 1.137 is whether the delay on the part of the party having the right or authority to reply to avoid abandonment was unavoidable or unintentional; where the applicant has assigned the entire right/title/interest, the applicant's delay is irrelevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a third party controls prosecution (assignee, licensee, etc.), the third party's decision whether to file a reply binds the applicant unless the third party is conducting prosecution only in a fiduciary capacity by express contract terms. Reassignment to the applicant prior to the due date for the reply can alter whose delay is relevant.
